name: Whitening powder (charcoal)

lead: Charcoal whitening powder is brushed onto teeth to lift surface stain, one of several consumer whitening formats alongside strips, pens and rinses. People use it for cleaner, lighter-looking teeth.

Proponents say the charcoal adsorbs and abrades stain from the enamel. It does not bleach internal tooth colour. Only a laboratory study of a related charcoal toothpaste and mouthwash on stained teeth was identified; no human trials were found.

paras: Users dip a damp brush in the powder and brush for a minute or two, a few times a week, sometimes alternating with regular toothpaste.
Whitening toothpastes in general contain more abrasives than regular ones, and the effect of charcoal on enamel has been examined in vitro. No clinical safety data were found.

angle.text: Users brush on activated charcoal powder to adsorb and abrade surface stain for cleaner, lighter-looking teeth, as one of several consumer whitening formats. Research on it is limited to laboratory work.

lead: Charcoal whitening powders are products of activated charcoal that users brush onto teeth with the aim of removing surface stain. They are one of several consumer whitening formats alongside strips, pens, rinses and toothpastes.

Wikipedia's tooth whitening article describes whitening toothpastes as containing more abrasives and detergents than regular ones, but its text does not cover charcoal powders specifically.[1] Dental research reviewed includes a laboratory study of a charcoal-containing toothpaste and mouthwash on stained canines.
No clinical studies of charcoal powders were identified.

paras: Users apply the powder with a wet toothbrush. Proponents say charcoal binds and lifts surface stains; no clinical source reviewed confirms this.

A 2020 in vitro study stained forty human canines with coffee and compared brushing with deionised water, regular toothpaste and charcoal-containing products over a simulated 90 days for colour change and enamel surface alteration.
